1	---
2	title: Models
3	description: 'Learn about the concepts for building your data model with Prisma: Models, scalar types, enums, attributes, functions, IDs, default values and more'
4	url: /orm/v7/prisma-schema/data-model/models
5	metaTitle: Models
6	metaDescription: 'Learn about the concepts for building your data model with Prisma: Models, scalar types, enums, attributes, functions, IDs, default values and more.'
7	---
8	
9	The data model definition part of the [Prisma schema](/orm/v7/prisma-schema/overview) defines your application models (also called **Prisma models**). Models:
10	
11	- Represent the **entities** of your application domain
12	- Map to the **tables** (relational databases like PostgreSQL) or **collections** (MongoDB) in your database
13	- Form the foundation of the **queries** available in the generated [Prisma Client API](/orm/v7/prisma-client/setup-and-configuration/introduction)
14	- When used with TypeScript, Prisma Client provides generated **type definitions** for your models and any [variations](/orm/v7/prisma-client/type-safety/operating-against-partial-structures-of-model-types) of them to make database access entirely type safe.
15	
16	The following schema describes a blogging platform - the data model definition is highlighted:
17	
18	```prisma highlight=10-46;normal tab="Relational databases"
19	datasource db {
20	  provider = "postgresql"
21	}
22	
23	generator client {
24	  provider = "prisma-client"
25	  output   = "./generated"
26	}
27	
28	model User { // [!code highlight]
29	  id      Int      @id @default(autoincrement()) // [!code highlight]
30	  email   String   @unique // [!code highlight]
31	  name    String? // [!code highlight]
32	  role    Role     @default(USER) // [!code highlight]
33	  posts   Post[] // [!code highlight]
34	  profile Profile? // [!code highlight]
35	} // [!code highlight]
36	
37	model Profile { // [!code highlight]
38	  id     Int    @id @default(autoincrement()) // [!code highlight]
39	  bio    String // [!code highlight]
40	  user   User   @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id]) // [!code highlight]
41	  userId Int    @unique // [!code highlight]
42	} // [!code highlight]
43	
44	model Post { // [!code highlight]
45	  id         Int        @id @default(autoincrement()) // [!code highlight]
46	  createdAt  DateTime   @default(now()) // [!code highlight]
47	  updatedAt  DateTime   @updatedAt // [!code highlight]
48	  title      String // [!code highlight]
49	  published  Boolean    @default(false) // [!code highlight]
50	  author     User       @relation(fields: [authorId], references: [id]) // [!code highlight]
51	  authorId   Int // [!code highlight]
52	  categories Category[] // [!code highlight]
53	} // [!code highlight]
54	
55	model Category { // [!code highlight]
56	  id    Int    @id @default(autoincrement()) // [!code highlight]
57	  name  String // [!code highlight]
58	  posts Post[] // [!code highlight]
59	} // [!code highlight]
60	
61	enum Role { // [!code highlight]
62	  USER // [!code highlight]
63	  ADMIN // [!code highlight]
64	} // [!code highlight]
65	```
66	
67	```prisma highlight=10-45;normal tab="MongoDB"
68	datasource db {
69	  provider = "mongodb"
70	  url      = env("DATABASE_URL")
71	}
72	
73	generator client {
74	  provider = "prisma-client-js"
75	}
76	
77	model User { // [!code highlight]
78	  id      String   @id @default(auto()) @map("_id") @db.ObjectId // [!code highlight]
79	  email   String   @unique // [!code highlight]
80	  name    String? // [!code highlight]
81	  role    Role     @default(USER) // [!code highlight]
82	  posts   Post[] // [!code highlight]
83	  profile Profile? // [!code highlight]
84	} // [!code highlight]
85	
86	model Profile { // [!code highlight]
87	  id     String @id @default(auto()) @map("_id") @db.ObjectId // [!code highlight]
88	  bio    String // [!code highlight]
89	  user   User   @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id]) // [!code highlight]
90	  userId String @unique @db.ObjectId // [!code highlight]
91	} // [!code highlight]
92	
93	model Post { // [!code highlight]
94	  id          String     @id @default(auto()) @map("_id") @db.ObjectId // [!code highlight]
95	  createdAt   DateTime   @default(now()) // [!code highlight]
96	  title       String // [!code highlight]
97	  published   Boolean    @default(false) // [!code highlight]
98	  author      User       @relation(fields: [authorId], references: [id]) // [!code highlight]
99	  authorId    String     @db.ObjectId // [!code highlight]
100	  categoryIDs String[]   @db.ObjectId // [!code highlight]
101	  categories  Category[] @relation(fields: [categoryIDs], references: [id]) // [!code highlight]
102	} // [!code highlight]
103	
104	model Category { // [!code highlight]
105	  id      String   @id @default(auto()) @map("_id") @db.ObjectId // [!code highlight]
106	  name    String // [!code highlight]
107	  postIDs String[] @db.ObjectId // [!code highlight]
108	  posts   Post[]   @relation(fields: [postIDs], references: [id]) // [!code highlight]
109	} // [!code highlight]
110	
111	enum Role { // [!code highlight]
112	  USER // [!code highlight]
113	  ADMIN
114	}
115	```
116	
117	The data model definition is made up of:
118	
119	- [Models](#defining-models) ([`model`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#model) primitives) that define a number of fields, including [relations between models](#relation-fields)
120	- [Enums](#defining-enums) ([`enum`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#enum) primitives) (if your connector supports Enums)
121	- [Attributes](#defining-attributes) and [functions](#using-functions) that change the behavior of fields and models
122	
123	The corresponding database looks like this:
124	
125	![Sample database](/img/orm/sample-database.png)
126	
127	<details>
128	
129	<summary>A model maps to the underlying structures of the data source.</summary>
130	
131	- In relational databases like PostgreSQL and MySQL, a `model` maps to a **table**
132	- In MongoDB, a `model` maps to a **collection**
133	
134	> **Note**: In the future there might be connectors for non-relational databases and other data sources. For example, for a REST API it would map to a _resource_.
135	
136	</details>
137	
138	The following query creates a `User` with nested `Post` and `Category` records:
139	
140	```ts
141	const user = await prisma.user.create({
142	  data: {
143	    email: "ariadne@prisma.io",
144	    name: "Ariadne",
145	    posts: {
146	      create: [
147	        {
148	          title: "My first day at Prisma",
149	          categories: { create: { name: "Office" } },
150	        },
151	        {
152	          title: "How to connect to a SQLite database",
153	          categories: { create: [{ name: "Databases" }, { name: "Tutorials" }] },
154	        },
155	      ],
156	    },
157	  },
158	});
159	```
160	
161	Your data model reflects _your_ application domain. For example:
162	
163	- In an **ecommerce** application you probably have models like `Customer`, `Order`, `Item` and `Invoice`.
164	- In a **social media** application you probably have models like `User`, `Post`, `Photo` and `Message`.
165	
166	## Introspection and migration
167	
168	There are two ways to define a data model:
169	
170	- **Write the data model manually and use Prisma Migrate**: You can write your data model manually and map it to your database using [Prisma Migrate](/orm/v7/prisma-migrate). In this case, the data model is the single source of truth for the models of your application.
171	- **Generate the data model via introspection**: When you have an existing database or prefer migrating your database schema with SQL, you generate the data model by [introspecting](/orm/v7/prisma-schema/introspection) your database. In this case, the database schema is the single source of truth for the models of your application.
172	
173	## Defining models
174	
175	Models represent the entities of your application domain. Models are represented by [`model`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#model) blocks and define a number of [fields](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#model-fields). In the example data model above, `User`, `Profile`, `Post` and `Category` are models.
176	
177	A blogging platform can be extended with the following models:
178	
179	```prisma
180	model Comment {
181	  // Fields
182	}
183	
184	model Tag {
185	  // Fields
186	}
187	```
188	
189	### Mapping model names to tables or collections
190	
191	Prisma model [naming conventions (singular form, PascalCase)](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#naming-conventions) do not always match table names in the database. A common approach for naming tables/collections in databases is to use plural form and [snake_case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snake_case) notation - for example: `comments`. When you introspect a database with a table named `comments`, the resulting Prisma model will look like this:
192	
193	```prisma
194	model comments {
195	  // Fields
196	}
197	```
198	
199	However, you can still adhere to the naming convention without renaming the underlying `comments` table in the database by using the [`@@map`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference) attribute:
200	
201	```prisma
202	model Comment {
203	  // Fields
204	
205	  @@map("comments")
206	}
207	```
208	
209	With this model definition, Prisma ORM automatically maps the `Comment` model to the `comments` table in the underlying database.
210	
211	> **Note**: You can also [`@map`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#map) a column name or enum value, and `@@map` an enum name.
212	
213	`@map` and `@@map` allow you to [tune the shape of your Prisma Client API](/orm/v7/prisma-client/setup-and-configuration/custom-model-and-field-names#using-map-and-map-to-rename-fields-and-models-in-the-prisma-client-api) by decoupling model and field names from table and column names in the underlying database.
214	
215	## Defining fields
216	
217	The properties of a model are called _fields_, which consist of:
218	
219	- A **[field name](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#model-fields)**
220	- A **[field type](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#model-fields)**
221	- Optional **[type modifiers](#type-modifiers)**
222	- Optional **[attributes](#defining-attributes)**, including [native database type attributes](#native-types-mapping)
223	
224	A field's type determines its _structure_, and fits into one of two categories:
225	
226	- [Scalar types](#scalar-fields) (includes [enums](#defining-enums)) that map to columns (relational databases) or document fields (MongoDB) - for example, [`String`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#string) or [`Int`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#int)
227	- Model types (the field is then called [relation field](/orm/v7/prisma-schema/data-model/relations#relation-fields)) - for example `Post` or `Comment[]`
228	
229	### Scalar fields
230	
231	The following example extends the `Comment` and `Tag` models with several scalar types. Some fields include [attributes](#defining-attributes):
232	
233	```prisma highlight=2-4,8;normal tab="Relational databases"
234	model Comment {
235	  id      Int    @id @default(autoincrement()) // [!code highlight]
236	  title   String // [!code highlight]
237	  content String // [!code highlight]
238	}
239	
240	model Tag {
241	  name String @id // [!code highlight]
242	}
243	```
244	
245	```prisma highlight=2-4,8;normal tab="MongoDB"
246	model Comment {
247	  id      String @id @default(auto()) @map("_id") @db.ObjectId // [!code highlight]
248	  title   String // [!code highlight]
249	  content String // [!code highlight]
250	}
251	
252	model Tag {
253	  name String @id @map("_id") // [!code highlight]
254	}
255	```
256	
257	See [complete list of scalar field types](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#model-field-scalar-types) .
258	
259	### Relation fields
260	
261	A relation field's type is another model - for example, a post (`Post`) can have multiple comments (`Comment[]`):
262	
263	```prisma highlight=4,10;normal tab="Relational databases"
264	model Post {
265	  id       Int       @id @default(autoincrement())
266	  // Other fields
267	  comments Comment[] // A post can have many comments // [!code highlight]
268	}
269	
270	model Comment {
271	  id     Int
272	  // Other fields
273	  post   Post @relation(fields: [postId], references: [id]) // A comment can have one post // [!code highlight]
274	  postId Int
275	}
276	```
277	
278	```prisma highlight=4,10;normal tab="MongoDB"
279	model Post {
280	  id       String    @id @default(auto()) @map("_id") @db.Objectid
281	  // Other fields
282	  comments Comment[] // A post can have many comments // [!code highlight]
283	}
284	
285	model Comment {
286	  id     String @id @default(auto()) @map("_id") @db.Objectid
287	  // Other fields
288	  post   Post   @relation(fields: [postId], references: [id]) // A comment can have one post // [!code highlight]
289	  postId String @db.ObjectId
290	}
291	```
292	
293	Refer to the [relations documentation](/orm/v7/prisma-schema/data-model/relations) for more examples and information about relationships between models.
294	
295	### Native types mapping
296	
297	**Native database type attributes** describe the underlying database type:
298	
299	```prisma
300	model Post {
301	  id      Int    @id
302	  title   String @db.VarChar(200)
303	  content String
304	}
305	```
306	
307	Type attributes are:
308	
309	- Specific to the underlying provider (e.g., PostgreSQL uses `@db.Boolean`, MySQL uses `@db.TinyInt(1)`)
310	- Written in PascalCase and prefixed by `@db`
311	- Only added during [introspection](/orm/v7/prisma-schema/introspection) if the native type differs from the default
312	
313	See [native database type attributes](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#model-field-scalar-types) for the complete list.
314	
315	### Type modifiers
316	
317	The type of a field can be modified by appending either of two modifiers:
318	
319	- [`[]`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#-modifier) Make a field a list
320	- [`?`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#-modifier-1) Make a field optional
321	
322	> **Note**: You **cannot** combine type modifiers - optional lists are not supported.
323	
324	#### Lists
325	
326	The following example includes a scalar list and a list of related models:
327	
328	```prisma
329	model Post {
330	  id       Int       @id @default(autoincrement())
331	  comments Comment[] // A list of comments
332	  keywords String[]  // A scalar list
333	}
334	```
335	
336	:::note
337	Scalar lists are only supported if the database connector supports them natively or at a Prisma ORM level.
338	:::
339	
340	#### Optional and mandatory fields
341	
342	```prisma
343	model Comment {
344	  id      Int     @id @default(autoincrement())
345	  title   String       // Required field
346	  content String?      // Optional field (nullable)
347	}
348	```
349	
350	Fields without `?` are required:
351	
352	- **Relational databases**: Represented via `NOT NULL` constraints
353	- **Prisma Client**: TypeScript types enforce these fields at compile time
354	
355	### Unsupported types
356	
357	When you introspect a relational database, unsupported data types are added as [`Unsupported`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#unsupported):
358	
359	```prisma
360	location    Unsupported("POLYGON")?
361	```
362	
363	Fields of type `Unsupported` don't appear in the generated Prisma Client API, but you can still use [raw database access](/orm/v7/prisma-client/using-raw-sql/raw-queries) to query them.
364	
365	:::note
366	The MongoDB connector doesn't support `Unsupported` types because it supports all scalar types.
367	:::
368	
369	## Defining attributes
370	
371	Attributes modify the behavior of fields or model blocks. The following example includes three field attributes ([`@id`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#id) , [`@default`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#default) , and [`@unique`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#unique) ) and one block attribute ([`@@unique`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference)):
372	
373	```prisma tab="Relational databases"
374	model User {
375	  id        Int     @id @default(autoincrement())
376	  firstName String
377	  lastName  String
378	  email     String  @unique
379	  isAdmin   Boolean @default(false)
380	
381	  @@unique([firstName, lastName])
382	}
383	```
384	
385	```prisma tab="MongoDB"
386	model User {
387	  id        String  @id @default(auto()) @map("_id") @db.ObjectId
388	  firstName String
389	  lastName  String
390	  email     String  @unique
391	  isAdmin   Boolean @default(false)
392	
393	  @@unique([firstName, lastName])
394	}
395	```
396	
397	Some attributes accept [arguments](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#attribute-argument-types) - for example, `@default` accepts `true` or `false`:
398	
399	```prisma
400	isAdmin   Boolean @default(false) // short form of @default(value: false)
401	```
402	
403	See [complete list of field and block attributes](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#attributes)
404	
405	### Defining an ID field
406	
407	An ID uniquely identifies individual records of a model. A model can only have _one_ ID:
408	
409	- In **relational databases**, the ID can be a single field or based on multiple fields. If a model does not have an `@id` or an `@@id`, you must define a mandatory `@unique` field or `@@unique` block instead.
410	- In **MongoDB**, an ID must be a single field that defines an `@id` attribute and a `@map("_id")` attribute.
411	
412	#### Defining IDs in relational databases
413	
414	In relational databases, an ID can be defined by a single field using the [`@id`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#id) attribute, or multiple fields using the [`@@id`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference) attribute.
415	
416	##### Single field IDs
417	
418	In the following example, the `User` ID is represented by the `id` integer field:
419	
420	```prisma highlight=2;normal
421	model User {
422	  id      Int      @id @default(autoincrement()) // [!code highlight]
423	  email   String   @unique
424	  name    String?
425	  role    Role     @default(USER)
426	  posts   Post[]
427	  profile Profile?
428	}
429	```
430	
431	##### Composite IDs
432	
433	In the following example, the `User` ID is represented by a combination of the `firstName` and `lastName` fields:
434	
435	```prisma highlight=7;normal
436	model User {
437	  firstName String
438	  lastName  String
439	  email     String  @unique
440	  isAdmin   Boolean @default(false)
441	
442	  @@id([firstName, lastName]) // [!code highlight]
443	}
444	```
445	
446	By default, the name of this field in Prisma Client queries will be `firstName_lastName`.
447	
448	You can also provide your own name for the composite ID using the [`@@id`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference) attribute's `name` field:
449	
450	```prisma highlight=7;normal
451	model User {
452	  firstName String
453	  lastName  String
454	  email     String  @unique
455	  isAdmin   Boolean @default(false)
456	
457	  @@id(name: "fullName", fields: [firstName, lastName]) // [!code highlight]
458	}
459	```
460	
461	The `firstName_lastName` field will now be named `fullName` instead.
462	
463	:::info
464	
465	Refer to the documentation on [working with composite IDs](/orm/v7/prisma-client/special-fields-and-types/working-with-composite-ids-and-constraints) to learn how to interact with a composite ID in Prisma Client.
466	
467	:::
468	
469	##### `@unique` fields as unique identifiers
470	
471	In the following example, users are uniquely identified by a `@unique` field. Because the `email` field functions as a unique identifier for the model (which is required), it must be mandatory:
472	
473	```prisma highlight=2;normal
474	model User {
475	  email   String   @unique // [!code highlight]
476	  name    String?
477	  role    Role     @default(USER)
478	  posts   Post[]
479	  profile Profile?
480	}
481	```
482	
483	:::info
484	
485	**Constraint names in relational databases** <br />
486	You can optionally define a [custom primary key constraint name](/orm/v7/prisma-schema/data-model/database-mapping#constraint-and-index-names) in the underlying database.
487	
488	:::
489	
490	#### Defining IDs in MongoDB
491	
492	The MongoDB connector has [specific rules for defining an ID field](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#mongodb) that differs from relational databases. An ID must be defined by a single field using the [`@id`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#id) attribute and must include `@map("_id")`.
493	
494	In the following example, the `User` ID is represented by the `id` string field that accepts an auto-generated `ObjectId`:
495	
496	```prisma highlight=2;normal
497	model User {
498	  id      String   @id @default(auto()) @map("_id") @db.ObjectId // [!code highlight]
499	  email   String   @unique
500	  name    String?
501	  role    Role     @default(USER)
502	  posts   Post[]
503	  profile Profile?
504	}
505	```
506	
507	In the following example, the `User` ID is represented by the `id` string field that accepts something other than an `ObjectId` - for example, a unique username:
508	
509	```prisma highlight=2;normal
510	model User {
511	  id      String   @id @map("_id") // [!code highlight]
512	  email   String   @unique
513	  name    String?
514	  role    Role     @default(USER)
515	  posts   Post[]
516	  profile Profile?
517	}
518	```
519	
520	:::warning
521	
522	**MongoDB does not support `@@id`**<br />
523	MongoDB does not support composite IDs, which means you cannot identify a model with a `@@id` block.
524	
525	:::
526	
527	### Defining a default value
528	
529	You can define default values for scalar fields using the [`@default`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#default) attribute:
530	
531	```prisma
532	model Post {
533	  id         Int        @id @default(autoincrement())
534	  createdAt  DateTime   @default(now())
535	  title      String
536	  published  Boolean    @default(false)
537	  data       Json       @default("{ \"hello\": \"world\" }")
538	}
539	```
540	
541	Default values can be:
542	
543	- **Static values**: `5` (`Int`), `"Hello"` (`String`), `false` (`Boolean`)
544	- **Lists**: `[5, 6, 8]` (`Int[]`), `["Hello", "Goodbye"]` (`String[]`)
545	- **Functions**: [`now()`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#now), [`uuid()`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#uuid), [`cuid()`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#cuid)
546	- **JSON**: Use escaped strings, e.g., `@default("{ \"hello\": \"world\" }")`
547	
548	See [attribute functions](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#attribute-functions) for connector support details.
549	
550	### Defining a unique field
551	
552	Unique attributes can be defined on a single field using [`@unique`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#unique), or on multiple fields using [`@@unique`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference):
553	
554	```prisma
555	model User {
556	  id    Int     @id @default(autoincrement())
557	  email String  @unique      // Single field unique
558	  name  String?
559	}
560	
561	model Post {
562	  id       Int    @id @default(autoincrement())
563	  title    String
564	  authorId Int
565	
566	  @@unique([authorId, title]) // Composite unique
567	}
568	```
569	
570	You can customize the constraint name with the `name` field: `@@unique(name: "authorTitle", [authorId, title])`
571	
572	See [working with composite unique identifiers](/orm/v7/prisma-client/special-fields-and-types/working-with-composite-ids-and-constraints) for Prisma Client usage.
573	
574	#### Composite type unique constraints (MongoDB)
575	
576	For MongoDB composite types, you can define unique constraints on nested fields:
577	
578	```prisma
579	type Address {
580	  street String
581	  number Int
582	}
583	
584	model User {
585	  id      Int     @id
586	  email   String
587	  address Address
588	
589	  @@unique([email, address.number])
590	}
591	```
592	
593	### Defining an index
594	
595	Define indexes via [`@@index`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#index):
596	
597	```prisma
598	model Post {
599	  id      Int     @id @default(autoincrement())
600	  title   String
601	  content String?
602	
603	  @@index([title, content])
604	}
605	```
606	
607	For MongoDB composite types, use dot notation: `@@index([address.city.name])`
608	
609	See [custom index names](/orm/v7/prisma-schema/data-model/database-mapping#constraint-and-index-names) for naming customization.
610	
611	## Defining enums
612	
613	Enums are defined via the [`enum`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#enum) block when [supported by your database](/orm/v7/reference/database-features#misc):
614	
615	```prisma
616	model User {
617	  id    Int     @id @default(autoincrement())
618	  email String  @unique
619	  name  String?
620	  role  Role    @default(USER)
621	}
622	
623	enum Role {
624	  USER
625	  ADMIN
626	}
627	```
628	
629	## Defining composite types (MongoDB)
630	
631	:::warning
632	Composite types are only available on MongoDB.
633	:::
634	
635	Composite types (embedded documents) allow embedding records inside other records:
636	
637	```prisma
638	model Product {
639	  id     String  @id @default(auto()) @map("_id") @db.ObjectId
640	  name   String
641	  photos Photo[]
642	}
643	
644	type Photo {
645	  height Int
646	  width  Int
647	  url    String
648	}
649	```
650	
651	**Supported attributes in composite types:** `@default`, `@map`, native types (`@db.ObjectId`)
652	
653	**Not supported:** `@unique`, `@id`, `@relation`, `@ignore`, `@updatedAt`
654	
655	## Using functions
656	
657	The Prisma schema supports [functions](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#attribute-functions) for default values:
658	
659	```prisma
660	model Post {
661	  id        Int      @id @default(autoincrement())
662	  createdAt DateTime @default(now())
663	  uuid      String   @default(uuid())
664	}
665	```
666	
667	Common functions: `now()`, `uuid()`, `cuid()`, `autoincrement()`, `auto()` (MongoDB ObjectId)
668	
669	## Relations
670	
671	See [relations documentation](/orm/v7/prisma-schema/data-model/relations) for relationship details.
672	
673	## Models in Prisma Client
674	
675	### Queries (CRUD)
676	
677	Every model generates CRUD queries in the [Prisma Client API](/orm/v7/prisma-client/setup-and-configuration/introduction):
678	
679	`findMany()` | `findFirst()` | `findUnique()` | `create()` | `update()` | `upsert()` | `delete()` | `createMany()` | `updateMany()` | `deleteMany()`
680	
681	Access via the lowercase model name property: `prisma.user.create({ ... })`
682	
683	### Type definitions
684	
685	Prisma Client generates TypeScript types for your models:
686	
687	```ts
688	export type User = {
689	  id: number;
690	  email: string;
691	  name: string | null;
692	};
693	```
694	
695	These types ensure type-safe database queries.
696	
697	## Limitations
698	
699	Every Prisma model must have at least one unique identifier:
700	
701	- `@id` or `@@id` for primary key
702	- `@unique` or `@@unique` for unique constraint
703

--- title: Models description: 'Learn about the concepts for building your data model with Prisma: Models, scalar types, enums, attributes, functions, IDs, default values and more' url: /orm/v7/prisma-schema/data-model/models metaTitle: Models metaDescription: 'Learn about the concepts for building your data model with Prisma: Models, scalar types, enums, attributes, functions, IDs, default values and more.' --- The data model definition part of the [Prisma schema](/orm/v7/prisma-schema/overview) defines your application models (also called **Prisma models**). Models: - Represent the **entities** of your application domain - Map to the **tables** (relational databases like PostgreSQL) or **collections** (MongoDB) in your database - Form the foundation of the **queries** available in the generated [Prisma Client API](/orm/v7/prisma-client/setup-and-configuration/introduction) - When used with TypeScript, Prisma Client provides generated **type definitions** for your models and any [variations](/orm/v7/prisma-client/type-safety/operating-against-partial-structures-of-model-types) of them to make database access entirely type safe. The following schema describes a blogging platform - the data model definition is highlighted: ```prisma highlight=10-46;normal tab="Relational databases" datasource db { provider = "postgresql" } generator client { provider = "prisma-client" output = "./generated" } model User { // [!code highlight] id Int @id @default(autoincrement()) // [!code highlight] email String @unique // [!code highlight] name String? // [!code highlight] role Role @default(USER) // [!code highlight] posts Post[] // [!code highlight] profile Profile? // [!code highlight] } // [!code highlight] model Profile { // [!code highlight] id Int @id @default(autoincrement()) // [!code highlight] bio String // [!code highlight] user User @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id]) // [!code highlight] userId Int @unique // [!code highlight] } // [!code highlight] model Post { // [!code highlight] id Int @id @default(autoincrement()) // [!code highlight] createdAt DateTime @default(now()) // [!code highlight] updatedAt DateTime @updatedAt // [!code highlight] title String // [!code highlight] published Boolean @default(false) // [!code highlight] author User @relation(fields: [authorId], references: [id]) // [!code highlight] authorId Int // [!code highlight] categories Category[] // [!code highlight] } // [!code highlight] model Category { // [!code highlight] id Int @id @default(autoincrement()) // [!code highlight] name String // [!code highlight] posts Post[] // [!code highlight] } // [!code highlight] enum Role { // [!code highlight] USER // [!code highlight] ADMIN // [!code highlight] } // [!code highlight] ``` ```prisma highlight=10-45;normal tab="MongoDB" datasource db { provider = "mongodb" url = env("DATABASE_URL") } generator client { provider = "prisma-client-js" } model User { // [!code highlight] id String @id @default(auto()) @map("_id") @db.ObjectId // [!code highlight] email String @unique // [!code highlight] name String? // [!code highlight] role Role @default(USER) // [!code highlight] posts Post[] // [!code highlight] profile Profile? // [!code highlight] } // [!code highlight] model Profile { // [!code highlight] id String @id @default(auto()) @map("_id") @db.ObjectId // [!code highlight] bio String // [!code highlight] user User @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id]) // [!code highlight] userId String @unique @db.ObjectId // [!code highlight] } // [!code highlight] model Post { // [!code highlight] id String @id @default(auto()) @map("_id") @db.ObjectId // [!code highlight] createdAt DateTime @default(now()) // [!code highlight] title String // [!code highlight] published Boolean @default(false) // [!code highlight] author User @relation(fields: [authorId], references: [id]) // [!code highlight] authorId String @db.ObjectId // [!code highlight] categoryIDs String[] @db.ObjectId // [!code highlight] categories Category[] @relation(fields: [categoryIDs], references: [id]) // [!code highlight] } // [!code highlight] model Category { // [!code highlight] id String @id @default(auto()) @map("_id") @db.ObjectId // [!code highlight] name String // [!code highlight] postIDs String[] @db.ObjectId // [!code highlight] posts Post[] @relation(fields: [postIDs], references: [id]) // [!code highlight] } // [!code highlight] enum Role { // [!code highlight] USER // [!code highlight] ADMIN } ``` The data model definition is made up of: - [Models](#defining-models) ([`model`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#model) primitives) that define a number of fields, including [relations between models](#relation-fields) - [Enums](#defining-enums) ([`enum`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#enum) primitives) (if your connector supports Enums) - [Attributes](#defining-attributes) and [functions](#using-functions) that change the behavior of fields and models The corresponding database looks like this: ![Sample database](/img/orm/sample-database.png)
A model maps to the underlying structures of the data source. - In relational databases like PostgreSQL and MySQL, a `model` maps to a **table** - In MongoDB, a `model` maps to a **collection** > **Note**: In the future there might be connectors for non-relational databases and other data sources. For example, for a REST API it would map to a _resource_.
The following query creates a `User` with nested `Post` and `Category` records: ```ts const user = await prisma.user.create({ data: { email: "ariadne@prisma.io", name: "Ariadne", posts: { create: [ { title: "My first day at Prisma", categories: { create: { name: "Office" } }, }, { title: "How to connect to a SQLite database", categories: { create: [{ name: "Databases" }, { name: "Tutorials" }] }, }, ], }, }, }); ``` Your data model reflects _your_ application domain. For example: - In an **ecommerce** application you probably have models like `Customer`, `Order`, `Item` and `Invoice`. - In a **social media** application you probably have models like `User`, `Post`, `Photo` and `Message`. ## Introspection and migration There are two ways to define a data model: - **Write the data model manually and use Prisma Migrate**: You can write your data model manually and map it to your database using [Prisma Migrate](/orm/v7/prisma-migrate). In this case, the data model is the single source of truth for the models of your application. - **Generate the data model via introspection**: When you have an existing database or prefer migrating your database schema with SQL, you generate the data model by [introspecting](/orm/v7/prisma-schema/introspection) your database. In this case, the database schema is the single source of truth for the models of your application. ## Defining models Models represent the entities of your application domain. Models are represented by [`model`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#model) blocks and define a number of [fields](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#model-fields). In the example data model above, `User`, `Profile`, `Post` and `Category` are models. A blogging platform can be extended with the following models: ```prisma model Comment { // Fields } model Tag { // Fields } ``` ### Mapping model names to tables or collections Prisma model [naming conventions (singular form, PascalCase)](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#naming-conventions) do not always match table names in the database. A common approach for naming tables/collections in databases is to use plural form and [snake_case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snake_case) notation - for example: `comments`. When you introspect a database with a table named `comments`, the resulting Prisma model will look like this: ```prisma model comments { // Fields } ``` However, you can still adhere to the naming convention without renaming the underlying `comments` table in the database by using the [`@@map`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference) attribute: ```prisma model Comment { // Fields @@map("comments") } ``` With this model definition, Prisma ORM automatically maps the `Comment` model to the `comments` table in the underlying database. > **Note**: You can also [`@map`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#map) a column name or enum value, and `@@map` an enum name. `@map` and `@@map` allow you to [tune the shape of your Prisma Client API](/orm/v7/prisma-client/setup-and-configuration/custom-model-and-field-names#using-map-and-map-to-rename-fields-and-models-in-the-prisma-client-api) by decoupling model and field names from table and column names in the underlying database. ## Defining fields The properties of a model are called _fields_, which consist of: - A **[field name](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#model-fields)** - A **[field type](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#model-fields)** - Optional **[type modifiers](#type-modifiers)** - Optional **[attributes](#defining-attributes)**, including [native database type attributes](#native-types-mapping) A field's type determines its _structure_, and fits into one of two categories: - [Scalar types](#scalar-fields) (includes [enums](#defining-enums)) that map to columns (relational databases) or document fields (MongoDB) - for example, [`String`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#string) or [`Int`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#int) - Model types (the field is then called [relation field](/orm/v7/prisma-schema/data-model/relations#relation-fields)) - for example `Post` or `Comment[]` ### Scalar fields The following example extends the `Comment` and `Tag` models with several scalar types. Some fields include [attributes](#defining-attributes): ```prisma highlight=2-4,8;normal tab="Relational databases" model Comment { id Int @id @default(autoincrement()) // [!code highlight] title String // [!code highlight] content String // [!code highlight] } model Tag { name String @id // [!code highlight] } ``` ```prisma highlight=2-4,8;normal tab="MongoDB" model Comment { id String @id @default(auto()) @map("_id") @db.ObjectId // [!code highlight] title String // [!code highlight] content String // [!code highlight] } model Tag { name String @id @map("_id") // [!code highlight] } ``` See [complete list of scalar field types](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#model-field-scalar-types) . ### Relation fields A relation field's type is another model - for example, a post (`Post`) can have multiple comments (`Comment[]`): ```prisma highlight=4,10;normal tab="Relational databases" model Post { id Int @id @default(autoincrement()) // Other fields comments Comment[] // A post can have many comments // [!code highlight] } model Comment { id Int // Other fields post Post @relation(fields: [postId], references: [id]) // A comment can have one post // [!code highlight] postId Int } ``` ```prisma highlight=4,10;normal tab="MongoDB" model Post { id String @id @default(auto()) @map("_id") @db.Objectid // Other fields comments Comment[] // A post can have many comments // [!code highlight] } model Comment { id String @id @default(auto()) @map("_id") @db.Objectid // Other fields post Post @relation(fields: [postId], references: [id]) // A comment can have one post // [!code highlight] postId String @db.ObjectId } ``` Refer to the [relations documentation](/orm/v7/prisma-schema/data-model/relations) for more examples and information about relationships between models. ### Native types mapping **Native database type attributes** describe the underlying database type: ```prisma model Post { id Int @id title String @db.VarChar(200) content String } ``` Type attributes are: - Specific to the underlying provider (e.g., PostgreSQL uses `@db.Boolean`, MySQL uses `@db.TinyInt(1)`) - Written in PascalCase and prefixed by `@db` - Only added during [introspection](/orm/v7/prisma-schema/introspection) if the native type differs from the default See [native database type attributes](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#model-field-scalar-types) for the complete list. ### Type modifiers The type of a field can be modified by appending either of two modifiers: - [`[]`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#-modifier) Make a field a list - [`?`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#-modifier-1) Make a field optional > **Note**: You **cannot** combine type modifiers - optional lists are not supported. #### Lists The following example includes a scalar list and a list of related models: ```prisma model Post { id Int @id @default(autoincrement()) comments Comment[] // A list of comments keywords String[] // A scalar list } ``` :::note Scalar lists are only supported if the database connector supports them natively or at a Prisma ORM level. ::: #### Optional and mandatory fields ```prisma model Comment { id Int @id @default(autoincrement()) title String // Required field content String? // Optional field (nullable) } ``` Fields without `?` are required: - **Relational databases**: Represented via `NOT NULL` constraints - **Prisma Client**: TypeScript types enforce these fields at compile time ### Unsupported types When you introspect a relational database, unsupported data types are added as [`Unsupported`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#unsupported): ```prisma location Unsupported("POLYGON")? ``` Fields of type `Unsupported` don't appear in the generated Prisma Client API, but you can still use [raw database access](/orm/v7/prisma-client/using-raw-sql/raw-queries) to query them. :::note The MongoDB connector doesn't support `Unsupported` types because it supports all scalar types. ::: ## Defining attributes Attributes modify the behavior of fields or model blocks. The following example includes three field attributes ([`@id`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#id) , [`@default`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#default) , and [`@unique`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#unique) ) and one block attribute ([`@@unique`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference)): ```prisma tab="Relational databases" model User { id Int @id @default(autoincrement()) firstName String lastName String email String @unique isAdmin Boolean @default(false) @@unique([firstName, lastName]) } ``` ```prisma tab="MongoDB" model User { id String @id @default(auto()) @map("_id") @db.ObjectId firstName String lastName String email String @unique isAdmin Boolean @default(false) @@unique([firstName, lastName]) } ``` Some attributes accept [arguments](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#attribute-argument-types) - for example, `@default` accepts `true` or `false`: ```prisma isAdmin Boolean @default(false) // short form of @default(value: false) ``` See [complete list of field and block attributes](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#attributes) ### Defining an ID field An ID uniquely identifies individual records of a model. A model can only have _one_ ID: - In **relational databases**, the ID can be a single field or based on multiple fields. If a model does not have an `@id` or an `@@id`, you must define a mandatory `@unique` field or `@@unique` block instead. - In **MongoDB**, an ID must be a single field that defines an `@id` attribute and a `@map("_id")` attribute. #### Defining IDs in relational databases In relational databases, an ID can be defined by a single field using the [`@id`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#id) attribute, or multiple fields using the [`@@id`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference) attribute. ##### Single field IDs In the following example, the `User` ID is represented by the `id` integer field: ```prisma highlight=2;normal model User { id Int @id @default(autoincrement()) // [!code highlight] email String @unique name String? role Role @default(USER) posts Post[] profile Profile? } ``` ##### Composite IDs In the following example, the `User` ID is represented by a combination of the `firstName` and `lastName` fields: ```prisma highlight=7;normal model User { firstName String lastName String email String @unique isAdmin Boolean @default(false) @@id([firstName, lastName]) // [!code highlight] } ``` By default, the name of this field in Prisma Client queries will be `firstName_lastName`. You can also provide your own name for the composite ID using the [`@@id`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference) attribute's `name` field: ```prisma highlight=7;normal model User { firstName String lastName String email String @unique isAdmin Boolean @default(false) @@id(name: "fullName", fields: [firstName, lastName]) // [!code highlight] } ``` The `firstName_lastName` field will now be named `fullName` instead. :::info Refer to the documentation on [working with composite IDs](/orm/v7/prisma-client/special-fields-and-types/working-with-composite-ids-and-constraints) to learn how to interact with a composite ID in Prisma Client. ::: ##### `@unique` fields as unique identifiers In the following example, users are uniquely identified by a `@unique` field. Because the `email` field functions as a unique identifier for the model (which is required), it must be mandatory: ```prisma highlight=2;normal model User { email String @unique // [!code highlight] name String? role Role @default(USER) posts Post[] profile Profile? } ``` :::info **Constraint names in relational databases**
You can optionally define a [custom primary key constraint name](/orm/v7/prisma-schema/data-model/database-mapping#constraint-and-index-names) in the underlying database. ::: #### Defining IDs in MongoDB The MongoDB connector has [specific rules for defining an ID field](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#mongodb) that differs from relational databases. An ID must be defined by a single field using the [`@id`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#id) attribute and must include `@map("_id")`. In the following example, the `User` ID is represented by the `id` string field that accepts an auto-generated `ObjectId`: ```prisma highlight=2;normal model User { id String @id @default(auto()) @map("_id") @db.ObjectId // [!code highlight] email String @unique name String? role Role @default(USER) posts Post[] profile Profile? } ``` In the following example, the `User` ID is represented by the `id` string field that accepts something other than an `ObjectId` - for example, a unique username: ```prisma highlight=2;normal model User { id String @id @map("_id") // [!code highlight] email String @unique name String? role Role @default(USER) posts Post[] profile Profile? } ``` :::warning **MongoDB does not support `@@id`**
MongoDB does not support composite IDs, which means you cannot identify a model with a `@@id` block. ::: ### Defining a default value You can define default values for scalar fields using the [`@default`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#default) attribute: ```prisma model Post { id Int @id @default(autoincrement()) createdAt DateTime @default(now()) title String published Boolean @default(false) data Json @default("{ \"hello\": \"world\" }") } ``` Default values can be: - **Static values**: `5` (`Int`), `"Hello"` (`String`), `false` (`Boolean`) - **Lists**: `[5, 6, 8]` (`Int[]`), `["Hello", "Goodbye"]` (`String[]`) - **Functions**: [`now()`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#now), [`uuid()`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#uuid), [`cuid()`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#cuid) - **JSON**: Use escaped strings, e.g., `@default("{ \"hello\": \"world\" }")` See [attribute functions](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#attribute-functions) for connector support details. ### Defining a unique field Unique attributes can be defined on a single field using [`@unique`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#unique), or on multiple fields using [`@@unique`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference): ```prisma model User { id Int @id @default(autoincrement()) email String @unique // Single field unique name String? } model Post { id Int @id @default(autoincrement()) title String authorId Int @@unique([authorId, title]) // Composite unique } ``` You can customize the constraint name with the `name` field: `@@unique(name: "authorTitle", [authorId, title])` See [working with composite unique identifiers](/orm/v7/prisma-client/special-fields-and-types/working-with-composite-ids-and-constraints) for Prisma Client usage. #### Composite type unique constraints (MongoDB) For MongoDB composite types, you can define unique constraints on nested fields: ```prisma type Address { street String number Int } model User { id Int @id email String address Address @@unique([email, address.number]) } ``` ### Defining an index Define indexes via [`@@index`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#index): ```prisma model Post { id Int @id @default(autoincrement()) title String content String? @@index([title, content]) } ``` For MongoDB composite types, use dot notation: `@@index([address.city.name])` See [custom index names](/orm/v7/prisma-schema/data-model/database-mapping#constraint-and-index-names) for naming customization. ## Defining enums Enums are defined via the [`enum`](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#enum) block when [supported by your database](/orm/v7/reference/database-features#misc): ```prisma model User { id Int @id @default(autoincrement()) email String @unique name String? role Role @default(USER) } enum Role { USER ADMIN } ``` ## Defining composite types (MongoDB) :::warning Composite types are only available on MongoDB. ::: Composite types (embedded documents) allow embedding records inside other records: ```prisma model Product { id String @id @default(auto()) @map("_id") @db.ObjectId name String photos Photo[] } type Photo { height Int width Int url String } ``` **Supported attributes in composite types:** `@default`, `@map`, native types (`@db.ObjectId`) **Not supported:** `@unique`, `@id`, `@relation`, `@ignore`, `@updatedAt` ## Using functions The Prisma schema supports [functions](/orm/v7/reference/prisma-schema-reference#attribute-functions) for default values: ```prisma model Post { id Int @id @default(autoincrement()) createdAt DateTime @default(now()) uuid String @default(uuid()) } ``` Common functions: `now()`, `uuid()`, `cuid()`, `autoincrement()`, `auto()` (MongoDB ObjectId) ## Relations See [relations documentation](/orm/v7/prisma-schema/data-model/relations) for relationship details. ## Models in Prisma Client ### Queries (CRUD) Every model generates CRUD queries in the [Prisma Client API](/orm/v7/prisma-client/setup-and-configuration/introduction): `findMany()` | `findFirst()` | `findUnique()` | `create()` | `update()` | `upsert()` | `delete()` | `createMany()` | `updateMany()` | `deleteMany()` Access via the lowercase model name property: `prisma.user.create({ ... })` ### Type definitions Prisma Client generates TypeScript types for your models: ```ts export type User = { id: number; email: string; name: string | null; }; ``` These types ensure type-safe database queries. ## Limitations Every Prisma model must have at least one unique identifier: - `@id` or `@@id` for primary key - `@unique` or `@@unique` for unique constraint
